title: Make Time
author: Jake Knapp & John Zeratsky
tagline: How to focus on what matters every day — from the designers who built Gmail's inbox and YouTube's binge engine.
oneLiner: You can't add hours, but you can design them: one Highlight a day, and a phone that works for you, not on you.
bigIdea: Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky — the Google designers behind time-management systems used by millions — wrote Make Time after realizing their own 'productivity' tools made them busier, not happier. Their system is radically simple: every day, pick ONE Highlight (the thing that matters most), make time for it with a laser (remove distractions), and energize yourself with real breaks (move, eat, sleep, unplug). The infinity pool — the endless feed of distractions — is the enemy; you can't quit it, but you can design around it.
quotes: Busy-ness is not a virtue; it's a trap.
The Highlight is the one thing you want to make sure happens today.
The infinity pool is the default state of modern life — the battle is to swim against it.

lessons.title: The Highlight: One Intention Per Day
lessons.summary: Every day, choose your Highlight: the one thing that, if it happens, makes the day a success. It can be urgent (a deadline), satisfying (a passion), or joyful (a person) — but it must be ONE, chosen deliberately in the morning, not discovered at midnight. The Highlight turns a reactive day into a designed day.
lessons.example: Knapp and Zeratsky's rule from their own lives: writing days began by picking the single chapter section that mattered most — everything else (email, meetings) was scheduled AROUND it, not before it. Days without a Highlight drifted into the infinity pool.
lessons.action: Tomorrow morning, write your Highlight in one sentence. Ask: 'Is this urgent, satisfying, or joyful?' Put it in your calendar for a fixed time.

lessons.title: The Laser: Design Out Distraction
lessons.summary: Once you have a Highlight, you need a laser: specific tactics to keep your attention on it. The authors' arsenal: phone in another room, browser with one tab, the 'busy' calendar block, headphones as a signal, and 'the phone stack' for meetings. The laser isn't willpower — it's design: you arrange the environment so focus is the default.
lessons.example: Their favorite: make your phone boring — delete social apps (or move them off the home screen), turn off every notification except humans. Knapp describes his phone as 'a brick that makes calls,' and his focus doubled.
lessons.action: Pick one laser tactic today: phone in another room during your Highlight, or notifications off for 2 hours. Do it for 5 days straight.

lessons.title: Energize: The Body Runs the Mind
lessons.summary: Focus is physical: a tired, hungry, motionless body can't sustain attention. The authors' energy rules: move every 90 minutes (exercise is the 'highlight multiplier'), eat real food (not sugar spikes), sleep 8 hours (the ultimate performance tool), and take genuine breaks — walking, not scrolling, because screens keep your attention working.
lessons.example: Knapp and Zeratsky both noticed their best ideas and focus came after exercise — so they scheduled workouts before hard work, not after. The authors also treat sleep like a competitive advantage, citing their own and others' data that tired days are lost days.
lessons.action: Add one energizer this week: a 10-minute walk before your Highlight, or a fixed bedtime 30 minutes earlier. Track your focus difference.

lessons.title: The Infinity Pool: Know Your Enemy
lessons.summary: The infinity pool is the endless feed — social media, news, video, the bottomless scroll — engineered by the smartest minds in the world to keep you swimming. The authors' warning: you can't win by willpower alone against products built by thousands of engineers. You win by design: making the pool hard to enter (log out, delete, move) and boring once you're in.
lessons.example: Both authors worked at Google on products that grew the pool (Gmail, YouTube) — which is exactly why they built Make Time: they knew the machinery from the inside, and knew the only defense is environmental.
lessons.action: Make one pool entry harder today: log out, delete the app, or put the phone across the room at night. Make one pool session shorter: set a 10-minute timer.

lessons.title: Design Days, Not Decades
lessons.summary: The book's final philosophy: don't chase a perfect system — run daily experiments. Each day, pick a Highlight, a laser tactic, and an energizer; at night, reflect on what worked ('highlight: yes, laser: failed, tomorrow: try the other room'). Small daily design beats grand yearly resolutions every time.
lessons.example: The authors literally rate their days and adjust one variable per day — a personal A/B testing loop. Their finding: people don't fail from lack of ambition; they fail from lack of daily design.
lessons.action: Tonight, write tomorrow's Highlight + one laser tactic + one energizer. Tomorrow night, rate each (1–5) and change exactly ONE thing.

lessons.title: Choose One Highlight Each Day and Protect It
lessons.summary: Knapp and Zeratsky's simple engine: each morning pick one 'highlight' — the single thing that will make the day count — then build the day around it, starting with it when possible. The highlight converts an infinite to-do list into a finite, winnable game. Busy is not the same as meaningful; the highlight is the meaning.
lessons.example: A manager who starts her day with one deep-work highlight — the report or decision that matters — protects it from the inbox and finishes it; days without a highlight vanish into meetings. The choice of one focus each morning is the whole method.
lessons.action: Every morning for a week, write one highlight sentence: 'Today will be a win if I...' — and do that before checking messages.

actionPlan: Pick a daily Highlight every morning — one sentence, scheduled.
Deploy one laser tactic daily for 5 days.
Add one energizer (walk, food, sleep) before your Highlight.
Make one infinity-pool entry harder today.
Run the daily A/B loop: rate Highlight, laser, energizer — change one thing.
caveat: Knapp & Zeratsky's 'make time for what matters' is the sanest focus system of the decade — and Argo AI is the corporate warning: a company that made time brilliantly — a decade of focus on one highlight, self-driving cars, backed by Ford and VW — and the highlight itself turned out to be a $3.6 billion dollar graveyard, because making time for the wrong highlight is still wasting time. The system's 'choose your highlight' step assumes you can pick correctly. Argo picked with total commitment; the market picked differently. Highlight wisely, and re-check the highlight against reality annually.
